title: Binder & IPC
scopeHtml: Scope: Binder model, driver and thread pool, oneway, Parcel/Parcelable/Bundle, the transaction buffer, AIDL, Messenger, cross-process bound services, death handling, caller identity and system services.

notes.title: The Binder model
notes.html:
What it is. Android apps live in separate processes that cannot touch each other's memory. Binder is the Android-specific mechanism that lets one process call a method on an object living in another process as if it were a local call. You call proxy.doThing(x); behind the scenes the arguments are flattened into bytes, the kernel carries them to the other process, a thread there runs the real method, and the result comes back.

Mechanism. Three roles: the client holds a proxy (IFoo.Stub.Proxy, a BinderProxy at the lowest level), the server holds the real object (a Binder subclass, IFoo.Stub), and the kernel binder driver (/dev/binder) moves the data and picks the receiving thread. Calls are synchronous by default: the calling thread blocks until the reply arrives. Binder gives one-copy transfer (data is copied once from sender to the receiver's mmap'ed buffer), per-call caller identity (UID/PID) that cannot be forged, and reference counting of remote objects with death notification.

Client process                 Kernel                    Server process
proxy.method(args)  --Parcel-->  /dev/binder  --copy--> Binder thread -> Stub.onTransact -> real method
      (blocked)     <--reply---                <--------

Why not sockets or pipes? Binder carries identity (UID/PID/SELinux context) that the kernel guarantees, supports passing object references and file descriptors, uses one copy instead of two, and has a thread pool model built in.

Real examples. Every startActivity, getSystemService(...) call, ContentResolver.query, LocationManager update and bindService is Binder. WebView renderers, Google Play services, and your own bound services talk over it.

Real-life picture. A bank counter with bulletproof glass: you pass a form through the slot, a clerk behind the glass handles it, and the guard stamps your ID on it so the clerk knows who really sent it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Binder is just "a socket". Its value is kernel-verified identity, one-copy transfer and object references.
  • Forgetting that calls block the caller by default, including on the main thread.
  • Thinking Binder works across devices; it is local only.

notes.title: Parcelable in IPC
notes.html:
What it is. A Parcelable is an object that knows how to write itself into, and read itself back from, a Parcel (a flat byte buffer). Anything passed over Binder (arguments, return values, Bundle contents) must be primitive-like or Parcelable.

Mechanism. writeToParcel(dest, flags) writes fields in order; CREATOR.createFromParcel(source) reads them in the same order. In Kotlin, @Parcelize generates both. A Parcel can also carry IBinder references and file descriptors (ParcelFileDescriptor), which is how objects and big data are passed safely. In AIDL, a custom type needs a parcelable Foo; declaration file, and parameters have a direction: in (copy to server), out (server fills, copied back), inout (both). Default to in; out and inout cost extra copies.

@Parcelize data class Order(val id: Long, val items: List<String>) : Parcelable

Pitfalls. Parcelable is not persistence: the layout is not versioned (see the Intent notes). Read order must match write order or you get garbage or BadParcelableException. Reading untrusted Parcels from other apps can be abused (type confusion, "Bundle mismatch" bugs where the reader and writer disagree about sizes), so prefer typed getters (API 33+) and validate lengths. Strings and lists cost bytes, and the whole payload counts toward the transaction buffer.

Real examples. Intent, Bundle, Message, Location, Notification and PendingIntent are Parcelable; Google Play services and Firebase SDKs pass Parcelable results to your process by Binder.

Real-life picture. Flat-pack furniture: the box lists how to pack and unpack it in strict order; if you rebuild in a different order, you get something odd.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Parcelable for disk storage or across app versions.
  • Mismatched write/read order after adding a field.
  • Using inout everywhere "to be safe".
  • Passing very large lists as a single Parcel.

notes.title: System services and ServiceManager
notes.html:
What it is. System services (ActivityManager, PackageManager, WindowManager, Location, Notification...) are Binder servers living mostly in system_server. Apps reach them through ServiceManager, a tiny naming service that is the phone book of Binder.

Mechanism. servicemanager is the first Binder object (handle 0), started by init. system_server registers each service by name (ServiceManager.addService("activity", ams)). Context.getSystemService(Context.ACTIVITY_SERVICE) returns a cached manager object (ActivityManager) wrapping a proxy obtained once via ServiceManager.getService("activity") (lookups are hidden API for apps; use getSystemService). Managers are cached per Context in SystemServiceRegistry. Since Android 8, vendor and HAL services use separate Binder domains (/dev/hwbinder, /dev/vndbinder) and AIDL HALs; servicemanager enforces SELinux rules on who may register or find a service.

Why it matters. Every manager call is an IPC with cost: a few tens to hundreds of microseconds when idle, much more if system_server is busy. Heavy use from hot paths (per-frame, per-scroll) or on the main thread adds jank. Permissions are enforced inside the service by checking the caller's UID.

Real examples. Calling PackageManager.getInstalledPackages() in a loop, or ActivityManager.getRunningAppProcesses() often, slows apps; TelephonyManager calls blocking the main thread appear as ANRs in Crashlytics; LayoutInflater/WindowManager are local wrappers that call remote services only for specific operations.

Real-life picture. A city information desk: it does not do the work, it just tells you which counter to go to, and you talk to that counter directly afterwards.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing getSystemService makes a new remote call each time.
  • Thinking system services run in your process.
  • Calling manager APIs on the main thread in hot paths.
  • Confusing servicemanager with ActivityManager.

notes.title: Binder threads and oneway
notes.html:
What it is. When a request arrives in the server process, it is handled on a Binder thread from that process's pool, not on the main thread. A oneway call is a fire-and-forget message: the caller does not wait for a reply.

Mechanism. The pool defaults to a maximum of 15 binder threads for apps (ProcessState::setThreadPoolMaxThreadCount, default 15 plus the main binder thread; system_server raises it to 31). The driver wakes an idle thread or asks the process to spawn one (BR_SPAWN_LOOPER) up to the max. These threads are named Binder:<pid>_N. Consequences:

  • Your service code runs concurrently on several threads: guard shared state.
  • It does not run on the main thread: touching views from it is a bug; post to the main handler if needed.
  • If all binder threads are busy (blocked on a slow operation or on a lock), new calls queue and callers hang, producing ANRs in client apps and eventually system_server stalls.
  • Nested/synchronous call chains across processes (A calls B calls A) can deadlock if they wait on the same busy thread pool; the driver tries to reuse the calling thread for the nested call from the same transaction chain.

oneway. Marked in AIDL (oneway void notify(in Event e); or a oneway interface). The call returns immediately after the data is queued in the target's buffer. No return value, no exceptions from the server. Calls to the same binder object are delivered in order (serialized per node, one at a time), but calls from different threads to different binders can be reordered relative to each other. Oneway has its own, smaller async buffer budget (half of the total), so floods are throttled (error "oneway spam" in logcat; Android 12+ detects it and can drop or log the spammer). Callbacks from a service to a client are typically oneway to avoid a slow client blocking the server.

Real examples. IApplicationThread calls from AMS to apps are oneway (lifecycle scheduleLaunchActivity), which keeps system_server from blocking on apps; broadcasts to receivers use oneway so a slow app does not stall delivery.

Real-life picture. A restaurant: a synchronous call is waiting at the counter until your food is ready; oneway is dropping a note in the order box and leaving. The kitchen has a limited number of cooks (binder threads); if they are all stuck, the queue grows.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming service methods run on the main thread.
  • Thinking oneway means no ordering at all; same-binder calls are ordered.
  • Doing slow I/O on binder threads.
  • Forgetting a oneway call cannot report errors back.

notes.title: The transaction buffer
notes.html:
What it is. Each process has one shared receive buffer for incoming Binder data, about 1 MB (BINDER_VM_SIZE = (1 MB) - 2 pages, i.e. about 1,016 KB for normal apps). All transactions currently in flight to that process share it, including oneway ones (which may use at most half of it).

Mechanism. The driver mmaps this region into the receiver; a sender's data is copied directly into it. If a Parcel does not fit, the transaction fails: the sender gets TransactionTooLargeException (a RemoteException subclass), and logcat shows !!! FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION !!! (parcel size = N). It can fail even for a modest Parcel if other transactions already fill the buffer.

Production incident (TransactionTooLargeException). Typical sources: large Bundles in onSaveInstanceState (crash at onStop, stack in ActivityThread.handleStopActivity / ActivityTaskManager), big Intent extras, a ContentProvider/service returning a big list, notification with a big RemoteViews bitmap, Messenger messages with huge Bundles. Diagnose by logging the Parcel size (Parcel.obtain(), writeBundle, dataSize()), AndroidX tooling, and reading the logcat line. Fixes: pass ids/URIs not data; paginate; persist to Room/files and share a content:// URI or ParcelFileDescriptor; shrink bitmaps for RemoteViews; keep only small ids in saved state (ViewModel plus disk for the rest); catch the exception at the boundary for non-critical calls.

Numbers to remember. About 1 MB total, shared; practical safe size per call is far smaller (tens of KB); crashes are reported on Android 7+ as exceptions rather than silent drops in some paths.

Real examples. Photo apps passing bitmap lists in extras, chat apps saving whole message lists in state, and widgets with big images all hit this; Google's guidance (and Crashlytics clusters of TransactionTooLargeException) pushes toward ids and disk.

Real-life picture. A single shared mail slot per building: one oversized parcel, or many parcels piled up, and nothing more fits through until the clerk clears it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the limit is 1 MB per call.
  • Looking at the line that adds the extra instead of onStop / the transaction that failed.
  • Catching the exception and ignoring lost data.
  • Thinking largeHeap raises this limit; it does not.

notes.title: AIDL basics
notes.html:
What it is. AIDL (Android Interface Definition Language) is a small file format where you describe an interface (methods, parameter types) and the build generates the Java/Kotlin (or C++/NDK/Rust) code for proxy and stub: the plumbing that turns a method call into a Parcel and back.

// IOrderService.aidl
package com.example;
import com.example.Order;
interface IOrderService {
    Order getOrder(long id);
    oneway void register(in IOrderListener listener);
}

Mechanism. The generated IOrderService.Stub extends Binder implements onTransact(code, data, reply, flags): it reads arguments from data, calls your implementation, and writes the result to reply. Stub.asInterface(IBinder) returns the real object if in the same process (no IPC, direct call) or a Stub.Proxy otherwise. Each method gets an integer transaction code in declaration order (FIRST_CALL_TRANSACTION + n) which is why reordering or inserting methods changes the wire protocol. Exceptions: Binder can carry a few (SecurityException, IllegalArgumentException, NullPointerException, IllegalStateException, UnsupportedOperationException, ServiceSpecificException); others cause a RuntimeException/crash on the server side. Enable AIDL in Gradle with buildFeatures { aidl = true }.

Using it. Server: Service.onBind() returns stub; client: bindService, then IOrderService.Stub.asInterface(binder) in onServiceConnected. Callbacks use a second AIDL interface (RemoteCallbackList<T> on the server manages listeners and removes dead ones automatically).

Real examples. Google Play Billing's IInAppBillingService, the Play Install Referrer, Custom Tabs ICustomTabsService, Google Play services APIs and Android's IActivityManager all are AIDL.

Real-life picture. A contract between two companies stating exactly what forms can be exchanged; a translator at each end converts the forms into the courier's envelope format.

Common interview traps.

  • Reordering methods in a published AIDL interface.
  • Doing UI work or long work directly in a stub method.
  • Forgetting asInterface skips IPC in the same process.
  • Leaking listeners instead of using RemoteCallbackList.

notes.title: Messenger versus AIDL
notes.html:
What it is. Two ways to build a bound service. A Messenger wraps a Handler: clients send Message objects, which are processed one at a time on the Handler's thread. AIDL exposes a full custom interface that can be called concurrently.

Aspect Messenger AIDL
Threading serialized on one Handler thread, no thread safety work multi-threaded, you synchronize
API shape what/arg/obj messages, Bundles typed methods, return values
Return values none directly; reply via replyTo Messenger direct returns, exceptions
Setup no AIDL file AIDL file + generated code
Throughput fine for light events better for frequent, typed calls
Versioning message codes + Bundle keys, flexible method signatures, stricter

Mechanism. Messenger(handler).binder is an IMessenger (an AIDL interface in the framework) whose only method is send(Message) (oneway). So Messenger is a thin, serialized, one-way layer over Binder.

Choosing. Messenger for simple, low-rate, cross-process commands where ordering and single-threadedness are wanted. AIDL for rich APIs, return values, high call rates or multiple concurrent clients. If the client and service are in the same process, use a local binder (extend Binder) or plain Kotlin instead of either.

Real examples. Old media apps and simple SDK-host communication use Messenger; Play Billing, Custom Tabs, and payment/identity SDKs use AIDL; OEM services typically AIDL.

Real-life picture. Messenger is a single-clerk mailbox: letters are handled one by one in order. AIDL is a phone line to a department that can answer several callers at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Messenger is multi-threaded.
  • Expecting a reply value from send.
  • Using either across processes when a local binder will do.
  • Putting huge Bundles in Messenger messages (same buffer limits).

notes.title: DeadObjectException and death recipients
notes.html:
What it is. If the process hosting a Binder object dies (crash, LMK kill, force stop), any proxy you hold becomes a "dead" handle. Calling it throws DeadObjectException (a RemoteException). A death recipient is a callback that the kernel triggers when the remote process dies, so you can react immediately.

Mechanism. The driver tracks death notifications (BC_REQUEST_DEATH_NOTIFICATION). In Java: binder.linkToDeath(recipient, 0); binderDied() is called on a Binder thread when the remote dies; unlinkToDeath when you no longer care. binder.isBinderAlive() / pingBinder() are polling alternatives (racy). For bound services, ServiceConnection.onServiceDisconnected() is called when the service process dies unexpectedly, but the binding stays and AMS will reconnect (onServiceConnected again) when the service restarts; onBindingDied() (API 28) / onNullBinding() signal when the binding itself is dead and you must unbindService and rebind.

Production incident (DeadObjectException). A client holds an IFoo proxy for a long time (cached in a singleton); the service process is killed in the background; the next call throws DeadObjectException and crashes if not caught, often showing up on specific OEMs with aggressive killers. Fixes: wrap remote calls in try/catch of RemoteException; treat the proxy as transient: on onServiceDisconnected/binderDied, clear it and rebind; retry idempotent calls with backoff; make operations idempotent; use RemoteCallbackList on the server to drop dead listeners; avoid caching raw IBinders beyond the connection's lifetime.

Real examples. Play services client libraries (GoogleApiClient/FusedLocationProviderClient) reconnect when Play services restarts; Custom Tabs and billing clients expose connection-state callbacks; media apps rebind to MediaBrowserService after kills.

Real-life picture. You hold a friend's phone number; when the friend moves city and the number is disconnected, calls fail at once; a death recipient is like a notification service that texts you the moment the number is cancelled.

Common interview traps.

  • Not catching RemoteException on every remote call.
  • Confusing onServiceDisconnected (process died, binding persists) with onBindingDied.
  • Forgetting unlinkToDeath, leaking the recipient.
  • Assuming the server will reply if it died mid-call; the caller gets DeadObjectException.

notes.title: Chatty IPC
notes.html:
What it is. Making many small Binder calls instead of a few bigger ones. Each call costs a context switch, a thread wake-up, copying and serialization; at scale this burns CPU, blocks threads and jank the UI.

Mechanism and numbers. A simple Binder round trip typically costs on the order of tens to a few hundred microseconds on a modern phone when idle (measure with Perfetto's binder_transaction slices; confirm on your device). Calls from the main thread to a busy system_server can take milliseconds and, in bad cases, seconds. 100 calls inside a 16 ms frame obviously cannot work. Perfetto/Systrace show "binder transaction" and "binder reply" slices linking client and server threads; adb shell dumpsys binder_calls_stats (debug) lists call counts per method.

Fixes (cost/perf optimization).

  • Batch: one call returning a list (getInstalledPackages once, ContentProviderOperation batches with applyBatch, bulkInsert).
  • Cache results in your process (package info, display metrics, system service managers) and invalidate by broadcasts/listeners.
  • Move off main thread; use Dispatchers.IO.
  • Push instead of poll: register a callback (NetworkCallback, registerContentObserver) instead of repeatedly querying.
  • Coalesce updates (debounce) and use oneway calls for notifications.
  • Avoid per-item IPC inside lists (ContentResolver.query per row, PackageManager.getApplicationLabel per row; load once).

Real examples. Launchers load icons and labels in bulk and cache them; Instagram/Facebook avoid per-frame WindowManager/PackageManager queries; contact-sync adapters use applyBatch for hundreds of rows.

Real-life picture. Going to the shop ten times for ten items instead of once with a list: the walking, not the items, is the cost.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimizing the payload when the real cost is the call count.
  • Polling a system service in a loop.
  • Doing synchronous IPC on the main thread.
  • Assuming local-looking calls (getSystemService().foo()) are free.

notes.title: Large payload IPC
notes.html:
What it is. The design question: how do you send megabytes (images, video frames, big lists) between processes when the transaction buffer is about 1 MB shared?

Options and trade-offs.

Approach How Notes
ParcelFileDescriptor / pipe ParcelFileDescriptor.createPipe(); pass the read side via Binder; stream data streaming, backpressure, simple; AutoCloseOutputStream
SharedMemory (API 27) / MemoryFile / ashmem map the same memory in both processes, pass the fd over Binder zero-copy, fast for frames/audio; you manage synchronization and lifetime
ContentProvider + openFile/content:// URI receiver reads a stream permission via URI grants (FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION), widely used
Files in shared/app storage write file, send path/URI simple but needs cleanup and permissions
HardwareBuffer / Surface share graphics buffers for camera/video/GPU pipelines
Chunking over Binder split into pieces under ~100 KB last resort, overhead and ordering to handle

Design considerations. Security (grant least privilege, validate the fd type/size, do not trust sender-declared lengths); lifecycle (close fds, delete temp files, handle process death mid-transfer); backpressure; versioning of the data format; memory (mmap counts in PSS "shared").

Real examples. Camera apps pass frames with HardwareBuffer/Surface; media players and MediaStore/DocumentsProvider pass files via fds; Google Photos shares images with editors through content URIs; Chrome passes shared memory regions between browser and renderer processes.

Real-life picture. Instead of squeezing a piano through the mail slot, you give the neighbour a key to the room where the piano already sits.

Common interview traps.

  • Chunking giant data through ordinary Binder calls.
  • Passing file paths instead of URIs/fds across apps (permission and FileUriExposed problems).
  • Forgetting to close the descriptor on both sides.
  • Using shared memory without synchronization.

notes.title: Caller identity and permissions
notes.html:
What it is. A service must know who is calling and whether that caller is allowed. Binder provides the caller's UID and PID reliably (the kernel stamps them), so permission checks can be trusted.

Mechanism. In a Binder method running on a binder thread: Binder.getCallingUid(), Binder.getCallingPid(). Helpers: Context.checkCallingPermission(perm) (checks the caller), enforceCallingPermission(perm, msg) (throws SecurityException), checkCallingOrSelfPermission, PackageManager.getPackagesForUid(uid) to map UID to package(s). Binder.clearCallingIdentity() returns a token that makes subsequent calls from your service look like they come from your own process, and restoreCallingIdentity(token) puts it back; use it in a try/finally when your service calls another service that checks permissions on your own identity, not the caller's.

override fun getSecret(): String {
    enforceCallingPermission("com.example.permission.READ_SECRET", "need READ_SECRET")
    val uid = Binder.getCallingUid()
    val token = Binder.clearCallingIdentity()
    try { return repo.load(uid) } finally { Binder.restoreCallingIdentity(token) }
}

Pitfalls. getCallingUid() is valid only on the binder thread during the call; after you hop to another thread it returns your own UID, so capture it first. checkCallingPermission returns false when called not from a Binder transaction (it then refers to your own process), a subtle bug in unit tests. A confused deputy arises if you act with your own privilege on behalf of an unauthorized caller. Prefer signature permissions for first-party components, check uid against an allowlist plus signature (PackageManager.checkSignatures), and never trust a package name passed as a parameter.

Real examples. ContentProviders check read/write permissions per URI; system_server services use enforceCallingOrSelfPermission(Manifest.permission.X); Play services verifies caller package + signature before returning a Google account token.

Real-life picture. A secure-building receptionist who checks the visitor's photo ID (UID) stamped by the guards at the door, not the name the visitor writes on a slip.

Common interview traps.

  • Trusting a package name or token argument for authorization.
  • Using getCallingUid() after switching threads.
  • Forgetting to restore the calling identity.
  • Using checkPermission with own identity so the check always passes.

notes.title: Exported service security
notes.html:
What it is. Post-incident theme: a bound or started service that is exported="true" (or has an intent filter) is callable by any app. If its methods perform sensitive work without checking the caller, any malicious app can use them.

Typical finding. A service exported for a partner app exposes an AIDL method like getUserToken() or setDebugMode(true) with no permission or caller check; or onBind returns the Binder for any intent; or it accepts a PendingIntent/Intent from the caller and fires it with the service's authority (intent redirection); or a leftover debug service was exported in release.

Fix checklist.

  1. android:exported="false" unless external access is a requirement; if external, protect with android:permission="..." using protectionLevel="signature" for same-developer apps (knownSigner on Android 12+ for partners).
  2. Check the caller in onBind/each method: Binder.getCallingUid() mapped to package + signature (allowlist), not a caller-supplied name.
  3. Validate and bound every input (sizes, enums, URIs); no Serializable from callers; typed getters.
  4. Keep the interface minimal: separate public AIDL from internal one; never expose raw files or tokens; return least data.
  5. Rate-limit and log abuse; use Context.enforceCallingPermission.
  6. Test with a hostile test app in CI; run lint (ExportedService), MobSF, and Play pre-launch security findings.
  7. On Android 11+ also review <queries> and visibility; on 14+ FOREGROUND_SERVICE type rules do not substitute for permissions.

Real examples. Public CVEs involve OEM and SDK services exposed with permissive AIDL (device-info or file-read methods); payment/OTP SDKs fixed by adding signature permissions and caller UID allowlists.

Real-life picture. A shop with a side door left open to the street and a staff-only cash drawer behind it with no lock: it works for the staff, and for everybody else too.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a custom permission protects when its protection level is normal.
  • Checking only package name, not signature.
  • Leaving debug services in release builds.
  • Thinking exported=false secures PendingIntents you handed out.

notes.title: Binder driver internals
notes.html:
What it is. The kernel side of Binder: a character device /dev/binder (plus /dev/hwbinder and /dev/vndbinder) that implements the transaction protocol via ioctl.

Mechanism.

  • Each process opens the driver and mmaps a receive buffer (about 1 MB). The driver keeps per-process state (binder_proc), per-thread state (binder_thread), and tracks objects as nodes (the real object, in the owner process) and refs/handles (client-side integers that map to nodes). Handle 0 is servicemanager.
  • A call is ioctl(BINDER_WRITE_READ) with commands such as BC_TRANSACTION / BC_REPLY; the receiver gets BR_TRANSACTION/BR_REPLY. copy_from_user copies the sender's Parcel once into a kernel buffer allocated inside the receiver's mmap'd region, so the receiver reads it in place (one copy total, versus two for sockets/pipes).
  • Object references and fds inside a Parcel are translated by the driver: it rewrites a node reference into a handle valid for the receiving process, and dup's a file descriptor into the receiver's table. Hence Binder references behave as capabilities.
  • Thread management: the driver picks a waiting thread of the target process (or reuses the caller's thread for nested calls), asks the process to spawn more via BR_SPAWN_LOOPER up to the max, and records sender_euid/sender_pid in the transaction for the receiver to read (getCallingUid).
  • Reference counting uses BC_INCREFS/ACQUIRE/RELEASE; death notifications use BC_REQUEST_DEATH_NOTIFICATION/BR_DEAD_BINDER.
  • Priority inheritance: the receiving binder thread temporarily inherits the caller's scheduling priority (nice) so high-priority callers are not stuck behind low-priority work. Async (oneway) transactions are queued per node, one at a time.
  • Android 11+ added the Binder freezer support: cached apps can be frozen (SIGSTOP-like cgroup freezer), and the driver rejects or flags calls to frozen processes (BINDER_FREEZE, sync calls to a frozen process return an error; oneway calls are queued, with a buffer limit).
  • Android 13/14 moved Binder to a Rust/binderfs model in parts; in recent kernels the driver can be built as binderfs mounts in containers (confirm in AOSP docs).

Observability. /sys/kernel/debug/binder/ (transactions, stats, failed_transaction_log), adb shell dumpsys binder, Perfetto binder slices (binder_transaction, binder_reply, binder_locked), logcat lines "binder: ... transaction failed".

Real examples. Perfetto traces of slow app starts show the app thread blocked in binder transaction into system_server (e.g. bindApplication); the "frozen app" logic of Android 11+ cached-app freezer explains DeadObject-like failures for frozen service calls.

Real-life picture. A postal sorting hub: the clerk copies your letter straight into the recipient's own pigeonhole (one copy), translates the sender's address into an internal code (handle), and writes the sender's verified ID on the envelope.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Binder copies twice. It copies once, into the receiver's mapped buffer.
  • Forgetting that handles are per-process integers, not global ids.
  • Ignoring priority inheritance when explaining why binder is real-time friendly.
  • Thinking the main thread of the server handles transactions.

notes.title: AIDL versioning and evolution
notes.html:
What it is. The migration scenario: your service and its clients are updated at different times (apps on user phones, partner SDKs), so the AIDL interface must evolve without breaking old clients or servers.

Why it breaks. The wire format is positional: transaction codes follow method order, and Parcelable fields follow write order. Inserting or reordering methods shifts the codes (old client calls the wrong method), removing a method breaks callers, and changing a Parcelable's field order or types corrupts data. Old servers receiving a new method code throw RemoteException/UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION.

Rules for safe evolution.

  1. Append only: add new methods at the end; never reorder, delete or change signatures of released ones (deprecate in docs).
  2. Add new fields to Parcelables at the end with a size/length prefix, or better use structured parcelables (AIDL-generated) which are more evolvable; the AIDL compiler can version stable AIDL (aidl_interface with frozen API snapshots, versions, in Android platform builds with stability: "vintf"), and provide getInterfaceVersion() / getInterfaceHash() to read the remote's version.
  3. Make the client check capability before calling a new method: if (service.version >= 3) service.newCall() or catch the failure; in newer AIDL (Android 11+ NDK/Java backends) calling an unknown method on an older server returns UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION / throws UnsupportedOperationException mapped by the generated stub.
  4. Use default implementations and feature flags; keep a negotiation call at connect (int getVersion() as the first method forever).
  5. For public SDK AIDL, keep a frozen copy per release in version control and check compatibility in CI (compare AIDL, or use Metalava-like API checks).
  6. Prefer new interface (IOrderServiceV2) for breaking changes and keep serving the old one for a transition window.
  7. Roll out: ship the server first (must tolerate old clients), then clients; staged rollout; monitor DeadObjectException, UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION, BadParcelableException, SecurityException rates by app version pair.

Real examples. Android platform's stable AIDL for HALs, Google Play Billing and Install Referrer evolving their IInAppBillingService by appending methods with a version parameter on each call (apiVersion), and Chrome Custom Tabs adding methods while checking feature support.

Real-life picture. Updating a printed menu that waiters already memorized by dish number: add new dishes at the end with new numbers; renumbering existing ones would send the wrong food to tables.

Common interview traps.

  • Inserting a new method in the middle of the interface.
  • Changing a Parcelable's field order or type.
  • Assuming client and server are always the same version.
  • Not providing a version handshake.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Binder is the Android IPC: proxy and stub, a kernel driver, a one-copy transfer, caller identity (UID/PID) stamped by the kernel, and object reference counting with death notification.
  • Calls are synchronous by default and run on a binder thread pool (about 15 threads per app, 31 in system_server), not the main thread; oneway returns immediately and is ordered per binder object.
  • The shared transaction buffer is about 1 MB per process; TransactionTooLargeException often fires at onStop from saved state: pass ids, URIs or file descriptors instead.
  • AIDL generates proxy and stub; method order and Parcelable field order are the wire format, so evolve append-only with a version handshake.
  • Messenger is a serialized, one-way Handler wrapper; AIDL is concurrent and typed.
  • DeadObjectException means the remote process died: catch RemoteException, use linkToDeath/onBindingDied, rebind and keep calls idempotent.
  • Chatty IPC is a cost: batch, cache, push instead of poll, move off the main thread.
  • Authorize with Binder.getCallingUid() and permissions, capture it before switching threads, use clearCallingIdentity carefully; never trust parameters for identity.
  • Exported services need signature permissions and caller checks; use ParcelFileDescriptor, SharedMemory or content URIs for big data.

questions.promptHtml: What is Binder, and why does Android use it for IPC instead of sockets, pipes or shared memory?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Almost every Android API you call (startActivity, getSystemService, ContentResolver) is a Binder call underneath. They want to see whether you know it exists and what it buys.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Binder is Android's kernel-backed RPC mechanism. A client holds a proxy to an object living in another process; calling a method on it is marshalled into a Parcel, sent through the /dev/binder driver (one copy into the target's mapped buffer), executed on a Binder thread in the server, and the reply comes back. Android picked it over sockets because the kernel stamps the caller's UID/PID on every transaction so identity cannot be forged, objects can be passed by reference with reference counting and death notification, and it costs one copy instead of two.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Android apps are separate Linux processes with separate UIDs, so any cross-app or app-to-system call needs IPC. The requirements were: (1) the server must know who is calling, reliably, to enforce permissions; (2) object references (not just bytes) must cross processes; (3) low latency and low copy overhead on phones; (4) lifecycle awareness (know when a peer dies).

 Client process                    Kernel                      Server process
 ┌──────────────┐  transact()  ┌─────────────┐  BR_TRANSACTION ┌────────────────┐
 │ Proxy        │─────────────>│ /dev/binder │────────────────>│ Binder thread  │
 │ (BinderProxy)│  Parcel      │ copies data │  data in server │ Stub.onTransact│
 │ thread BLOCKS│<─────────────│ 1 copy into │<────────────────│ runs your code │
 └──────────────┘  reply       │ server mmap │  BC_REPLY       └────────────────┘
                               │ + stamps    │
                               │ UID / PID   │
                               └─────────────┘

Comparison:

Mechanism Copies Caller identity Object refs / death notify Sync RPC semantics
Unix socket 2 (user to kernel to user) SO_PEERCRED possible but manual No You build it
Pipe 2 No No No
Shared memory 0 No No No (needs your own locking)
Binder 1 Kernel-enforced, unforgeable Yes (refcounts, linkToDeath) Yes, built in

Key properties:

  • Identity: Binder.getCallingUid() is set by the kernel, not by the client. This is the foundation of the Android permission model.
  • Object references: an IBinder passed in a Parcel arrives as a proxy in the receiver. Passing a callback interface to a service works because of this.
  • Synchronous by default: the calling thread blocks until the server replies. oneway makes it fire-and-forget.
  • Thread pool: the server process runs a pool of Binder threads; you do not manage sockets or accept loops.
  • Every system service (ActivityManager, PackageManager, WindowManager) is reached through Binder; servicemanager (handle 0) is the name registry.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(what a framework call looks like conceptually; you never write this by hand)

// This innocent call is a synchronous Binder transaction to system_server.
val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
val info = ActivityManager.MemoryInfo()
am.getMemoryInfo(info) // ActivityManager -> IActivityManager.Proxy -> Binder -> AMS

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Binder is just AIDL". AIDL is a code generator on top; Binder is the kernel driver plus libbinder.
  • Claiming Binder is zero-copy. It is one copy (shared memory via ashmem/memfd is the zero-copy path).
  • Forgetting that calls are synchronous and can block the UI thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does the server know who called? → The driver attaches sender UID/PID to the transaction; read via Binder.getCallingUid() on the Binder thread.
  2. Does a method call within the same process go through the driver? → No. Stub.asInterface() returns the local object when the binder is in-process, so it is a plain method call.
  3. What is handle 0? → The context manager, servicemanager, which maps service names to binder references; every process can reach it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "IPC mechanism, used with AIDL/services". The senior answer explains why: kernel-verified UID, one-copy transfer, reference passing and death notification, and then connects it to practical consequences (blocking calls, 1 MB buffer, thread pool limits).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams routinely discover that "innocent" Manager calls on the main thread are Binder round-trips that stall when system_server is busy; understanding Binder is what lets you read those Perfetto slices.

questions.promptHtml: Parcelable vs Serializable: which do you use on Android and why? How does @Parcelize work, and can you persist a Parcel to disk?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the Parcel is the IPC wire format, not a storage format, and whether you use the tooling correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Parcelable, because it is designed for Binder marshalling: explicit field-by-field writes with no reflection, so it is faster and produces smaller payloads than Serializable. In Kotlin I use @Parcelize from the kotlin-parcelize plugin, which generates writeToParcel and the CREATOR. A Parcel must never be persisted: the format is not stable across OS versions and is not meant for storage; use a database, protobuf or JSON for that.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Parcel is a flat, in-memory buffer of primitives and object references (including file descriptors and IBinders, which Serializable cannot carry). The reader must read in exactly the order the writer wrote.
  • Serializable uses Java reflection and writes class metadata and field names into the stream, which costs CPU and bytes. Parcelable writes only values.
  • @Parcelize generates the same code you would write by hand. Only primary constructor properties are written; body properties are not, so they come back as defaults (the IDE warns).
  • Unsupported field types need @RawValue (works only if the value is itself Parcelable/Serializable at runtime, otherwise it throws at write time) or a custom Parceler.
  • Bundle is a typed key-value map backed by a Parcel; it is lazily unparcelled on first access, which is why a bad class can crash on getX() rather than at the sender.
  • Since API 33, the typed Bundle.getParcelable(key, Clazz) overloads exist and the untyped ones are deprecated; use BundleCompat/IntentCompat from androidx.core for older devices.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts: id("kotlin-parcelize")
import android.os.Parcelable
import kotlinx.parcelize.IgnoredOnParcel
import kotlinx.parcelize.Parcelize

@Parcelize
data class Order(
    val id: String,
    val lines: List<Line>,       // Line must also be Parcelable
) : Parcelable {
    @IgnoredOnParcel
    var uiExpanded: Boolean = false   // body property: NOT written, resets after IPC
}

@Parcelize
data class Line(val sku: String, val qty: Int) : Parcelable

// Reading safely on API 33+ and below
val order = IntentCompat.getParcelableExtra(intent, "order", Order::class.java)

Broken: parcel.marshall() to a file, then unmarshall() after an app update.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing and reading fields in different order in hand-written Parcelables (silent corruption or crash).
  • Putting a non-Parcelable via @RawValue and crashing at runtime.
  • Persisting Parcel bytes (shared prefs, DB, disk cache). Framework classes inside change between releases.
  • Passing huge lists through Intent extras (see the transaction buffer question).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Serializable slower? → Reflection, per-object stream headers, and boxing; plus larger bytes means more of the Binder buffer.
  2. What happens to a Parcelable Bundle sent to another app that lacks your class? → BadParcelableException/ClassNotFoundException when the receiver unparcels it.
  3. Is Parcel safe to trust from another app? → No; the Parcel contents are attacker-controlled input in exported components (type confusion, mismatched Parcel bugs have been a real CVE class).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Parcelable is faster". Senior adds: why (no reflection, FDs and Binders supported), the primary-constructor-only rule, not-for-persistence, lazy Bundle unparcelling, and the security angle of untrusted Parcels.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team stored a Parcel-marshalled draft in a file; after an OS upgrade the layout changed and every user crashed on launch reading the draft.

questions.promptHtml: What does context.getSystemService(...) actually return, and how does it reach a service living in system_server?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand the Manager/proxy pattern and that "system service" calls are IPC.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It returns a client-side Manager object, for example ActivityManager or ConnectivityManager. The Manager wraps an AIDL proxy to the real service, whose IBinder was fetched from servicemanager by name. SystemServiceRegistry creates and caches these managers per Context, so most methods you call are Binder transactions into system_server.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
getSystemService(X)
  -> ContextImpl.getSystemService
  -> SystemServiceRegistry.getSystemService(ctx, name)
       fetcher (cached) -> new XManager(ctx, IX.Stub.asInterface(
                              ServiceManager.getServiceOrThrow(name)))
  -> XManager.method() -> IX proxy -> Binder -> service in system_server
  • Registration happens statically in SystemServiceRegistry with fetcher types: CachedServiceFetcher (one per ContextImpl), StaticServiceFetcher (one per process), StaticApplicationContextServiceFetcher.
  • The Manager is mostly a thin facade: it adds API-level checks, converts exceptions (RemoteException to rethrowFromSystemServer) and sometimes caches.
  • Apps cannot call ServiceManager directly (hidden API, SELinux restricts which services an app domain can look up).
  • Context matters. Some services depend on the Context: WINDOW_SERVICE and LAYOUT_INFLATER_SERVICE are themed/display-aware when obtained from an Activity. From API 30, StrictMode detectIncorrectContextUse() flags getting UI-related services from the Application context.
  • It can return null when a service does not exist on the device (for example missing hardware).
  • If system_server dies, the next call throws DeadSystemException, and the system effectively reboots the framework.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val cm = getSystemService(ConnectivityManager::class.java) // type-safe form, preferred
val wm = activity.getSystemService(WindowManager::class.java) // use Activity for UI services

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Obtaining WindowManager/LayoutInflater from applicationContext and getting unthemed/wrong-display results.
  • Assuming getters are cheap and calling them in tight loops on the main thread (each can be a Binder round-trip).
  • Not null-checking on optional hardware services.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the Manager the same object each call? → For a given ContextImpl it is cached, so mostly yes; across Contexts, no.
  2. Which thread executes the service code? → A Binder thread in system_server, not your thread.
  3. What if the service is slow? → Your calling thread blocks; do not call these on the main thread in hot paths.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE knows it is "how you get the system service". Senior describes the registry/fetcher/proxy chain, Context sensitivity, and the fact that each call is a blocking IPC.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup regression traced to calling PackageManager and ActivityManager getters hundreds of times during init; each one was a Binder hop.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the Binder thread pool and the oneway keyword. What happens if all Binder threads in a process are busy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know calls are synchronous and bounded in concurrency from those who treat IPC as free.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each process gets a pool of Binder threads, by default about 15 spawned plus the initial one, commonly quoted as 16. Incoming transactions run on those threads, not on your main thread. A normal call blocks the caller until the reply; oneway returns immediately, has no return value, and calls on the same binder object are delivered in order. If every Binder thread is busy, new incoming transactions queue in the driver and callers appear to hang, potentially cascading into ANRs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The driver asks userspace to spawn more looper threads (BR_SPAWN_LOOPER) when there are no free threads and the count is below max. Threads show up in traces as Binder:<pid>_1 ... Binder:<pid>_F (hex).
  • Your Stub.onTransact and your implementation run on those threads, so server code must be thread-safe and must not block for long.
  • Synchronous call: the client thread parks in the driver. Priority inheritance: the driver can raise the Binder thread's priority to the caller's, which is useful when the caller is the UI thread.
  • Nested/reverse calls: if A calls B and B calls back A while A's thread is blocked, the driver reuses A's blocked thread for the callback, avoiding deadlock for same-thread recursion.
  • oneway: void only, no exceptions propagated from the server. Ordering is guaranteed per binder object, not across different objects. Oneway transactions use only about half of the transaction buffer (the "async space"), so floods of oneway calls fail earlier than sync ones. Since Android 11-12 the platform detects "oneway spam" and logs it; treat that as a bug.
  • Deadlock scenario: server holds lock L and calls out synchronously to a client; the client calls back into the server on a Binder thread that waits for L. Classic Binder deadlock. Never call out to clients while holding a lock.
  • Exhaustion: a slow method (disk, network, lock wait) on the server, called by many clients, can saturate all threads; unrelated, fast calls then stall behind it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// IMetrics.aidl
oneway interface IMetrics {
    void log(in String event);   // fire-and-forget, ordered per binder object
}
interface IStore {
    String get(String key);       // blocking, caller waits
    oneway void invalidate();     // may return before work runs
}
// Server side: thread-safe by construction
private val store = ConcurrentHashMap<String, String>()
override fun get(key: String): String? = store[key]   // runs on a Binder thread

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing blocking I/O inside a Stub method (starves the pool).
  • Mutating shared state in the Stub without synchronisation.
  • Assuming oneway means "no cost"; it still consumes async buffer and can be lost if the process dies.
  • Calling a client callback while holding a lock.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you change the pool size? → Not through a public API; the hidden setMaxThreads exists in the framework. Design for the default instead.
  2. How do you see Binder thread saturation? → Thread dump/ANR trace showing all Binder: threads blocked, Perfetto binder slices, and dumpsys of Binder state on debuggable setups.
  3. Are oneway calls across two different binder objects ordered? → No, only per object.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "oneway is async". Senior adds ordering scope, async buffer halving, thread-safety, lock-ordering deadlocks, and the saturation failure mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared analytics service in a sibling process held a lock during file I/O; clients' main threads waited on it and showed up as ANRs in the clients, not in the service.

questions.promptHtml: What is the 1 MB Binder transaction buffer limit? What exactly is shared, what throws, and what are the non-obvious ways to blow through it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: TransactionTooLargeException is one of the most common platform crashes; interviewers want the mechanism, not "keep Bundles small".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each process gets one mapped Binder buffer of about 1 MB (1 MB minus two pages, so roughly 1016 KB with 4 KB pages). That buffer is shared by all transactions currently in flight for the process, not per call. If a transaction cannot get space, you get TransactionTooLargeException (a RemoteException), and logcat shows "FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION". Intent extras, saved-state Bundles, fragment arguments and large IPC returns all count.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The buffer is mapped at process start (ProcessState mmap). The driver copies each incoming transaction into the receiving process's buffer. The size is a process-wide pool, so 10 concurrent 200 KB transactions already exhaust it even though each is "small".
  • Oneway (async) transactions may use only about half (about 508 KB).
  • The limit applies to parcel size, which is bigger than your logical data: Strings are UTF-16 in Parcel (2 bytes per char, plus length and padding), Bundles add keys and type tags, object offsets add overhead. A 600 KB JSON string is about 1.2 MB in a Parcel, so it fails.
  • Where it bites in apps:
    • startActivity with big extras (Intent goes to system_server).
    • Activity stop / onSaveInstanceState: the whole saved Bundle (activity, view hierarchy, every fragment's state and arguments) is sent to system_server. Since Android 7 (API 24), this happens when the Activity stops, and failure surfaces as a crash in the background.
    • Notification, RemoteViews/widget updates containing Bitmaps.
    • Bound-service AIDL calls returning large lists.
  • Platform APIs that return big lists use ParceledListSlice, which chunks results over multiple transactions to stay under the limit; your own AIDL does not get that for free.
  • Cursor results through ContentProvider use CursorWindow (ashmem, about 2 MB window default), a different mechanism that fails with different symptoms.
  • Rule of thumb: keep saved state in the tens of KB (Android's saved-state guidance says to store only small, UI-restoration data).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: whole result set in saved state
override fun onSaveInstanceState(out: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(out)
    out.putParcelableArrayList("items", ArrayList(items)) // 8,000 items * ~300 B -> multi-MB parcel
}
// Fix: keep IDs / cursor position; reload from Room/network on restore
override fun onSaveInstanceState(out: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(out)
    out.putString("selectedId", selectedId)
    out.putInt("scrollPos", scrollPos)
}

Diagnose size quickly:

fun Bundle.sizeBytes(): Int {
    val p = android.os.Parcel.obtain()
    try { p.writeBundle(this); return p.dataSize() } finally { p.recycle() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Catching TransactionTooLargeException around startActivity and ignoring the real cause.
  • Assuming the limit is per call, not per process pool.
  • Putting Bitmaps or Serializable blobs in extras.
  • Blaming only your Activity; fragments, View.onSaveInstanceState (for example big EditText text, RecyclerView adapters with state) also contribute.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a 400 KB Bundle fail? → Other transactions are in flight, parcel overhead (UTF-16 strings), and several Bundles are saved at once.
  2. How do you pass a 5 MB blob to another process? → File/ContentProvider with ParcelFileDescriptor, or SharedMemory; send only a handle through Binder.
  3. Does SavedStateHandle/ViewModel avoid it? → ViewModel itself lives in-process (not in the Bundle). SavedStateHandle contents do go into the saved Bundle, so the limit applies to them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "1 MB limit, don't pass big data". Senior: process-wide shared pool, async half, parcel overhead math, background crash timing since API 24, and concrete alternatives (IDs, files, shared memory).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout flow saved the full cart (with product descriptions) in state; crash rate spiked only for users with 40+ items, on devices where the Activity was stopped.

questions.promptHtml: How does AIDL work? What does the generated code look like, what do in/out/inout mean, and what threading rules apply?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can design a cross-process API correctly and understand what the tool is generating.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: AIDL is an interface definition language; the tool generates a Java interface plus two classes: Stub (server side, extends Binder, implements onTransact that unmarshals the Parcel and calls your implementation) and Proxy (client side, marshals arguments and calls transact). asInterface() returns the local object in-process or a Proxy otherwise. Non-primitive parameters need a direction tag (in, out, inout), and server methods run on Binder pool threads, so they must be thread-safe.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client                                   Server
 IFoo foo = IFoo.Stub.asInterface(b)      class Impl : IFoo.Stub()
   |  (Proxy)                                 ^
   | foo.add(1,2)                             | onTransact(code=1, data, reply)
   v                                          |   unmarshal -> Impl.add(1,2) -> write result
 mRemote.transact(code=1, data, reply, 0) ----+
  • Transaction codes are FIRST_CALL_TRANSACTION + index of the method in the file. Reordering or inserting methods changes codes: a version-skew landmine (see the AIDL evolution scenario).
  • Direction tags: in (copied to server; default for primitives, String, IBinder), out (server fills a fresh object; copied back), inout (both). out/inout costs extra marshalling and require non-final, creatable types. Prefer in plus return values.
  • Types: primitives, String, CharSequence, List/Map of supported types, Parcelables (declared in a .aidl file), other AIDL interfaces (arrive as proxies; the callback pattern), IBinder, FDs through ParcelFileDescriptor.
  • oneway: void methods, async.
  • Errors: Exceptions thrown in the server are marshalled only for a small set (SecurityException, IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, NullPointerException, UnsupportedOperationException, ...) and rethrown in the client. Other exceptions crash the server's Binder thread and the client sees a RemoteException or the server process crashes; do not rely on custom exceptions.
  • Build setup: android { buildFeatures { aidl = true } }, files under src/main/aidl, package-matched.
  • Same-process: asInterface returns the Stub directly (no Binder, caller's thread, no copies, and mutations visible!). This difference between local and remote behaviour surprises people with out params and shared mutable objects.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// src/main/aidl/com/acme/IRecorder.aidl
package com.acme;
import com.acme.RecordingInfo;        // parcelable declared in RecordingInfo.aidl
import com.acme.IRecorderCallback;

interface IRecorder {
    int apiVersion();                                  // first, never moves
    void start(in RecordingInfo info, IRecorderCallback cb);
    oneway void stop();
}
class RecorderService : Service() {
    private val impl = object : IRecorder.Stub() {
        override fun apiVersion() = 1
        override fun start(info: RecordingInfo, cb: IRecorderCallback) { /* binder thread! */ }
        override fun stop() { /* oneway: caller already gone */ }
    }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent): IBinder = impl
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting thread-safety; touching UI or main-thread-only state from start().
  • Using inout everywhere "to be safe".
  • Reordering methods in a published AIDL, shifting transaction codes.
  • Throwing a custom exception expecting the client to catch it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can the client call you back? → Pass an AIDL callback interface as a parameter; the server holds the proxy and calls it (use RemoteCallbackList).
  2. What happens when the client process is in the same process as the service? → No IPC; direct calls on the caller's thread.
  3. How do you version it? → Append-only methods, a leading apiVersion() method, Bundle-based or length-prefixed parcelables, and tests that diff the AIDL against a golden copy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE can write an AIDL file and bind. Senior knows Stub/Proxy internals, transaction code ordering, direction costs, threading, exception marshalling limits and versioning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A vendor SDK shipped a new AIDL with a method inserted mid-file; old host apps executed the wrong method for weeks before anyone noticed.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app (1.2M DAU, 70% Android) ships v8.4. Crashlytics shows a new crash cluster, 0.9% of sessions (up from 0.1%), almost all on Android 8-13:

java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1187532 bytes
    at android.app.servertransaction.PendingTransactionActions$StopInfo.run
Caused by: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1187532 bytes

Logcat on a repro device also prints !!! FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION !!! (parcel size = 1187532). Crashes occur when users press Home or open another app, not while using the screen. v8.4 added "recently viewed" carousel and a filter screen. Product says "we did not touch navigation or startActivity". Big-memory flagship devices are affected as much as low-end ones.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find the cause and fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the Binder buffer" or "wrap in try/catch" (neither is possible), or "it must be our Intent extras" without checking where the stack points. Also blaming memory because "it is an OOM-like crash on big data".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Is the crash on foreground or when the Activity stops? The stack (StopInfo) says stop, which points at saved state, not startActivity. (b) Which screens are on top at crash time (Crashlytics breadcrumbs/custom keys)? (c) Does it correlate with account size, for example users with long histories? That suggests data-dependent growth. (d) What changed in v8.4 in state: new fragments, new onSaveInstanceState, new adapters?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce blast radius: remote-config kill switch for the new carousel if it is part of state; stage rollout to 20% halt. If a hotfix is needed, strip the biggest key from saved state.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) A list of objects placed in a Bundle (putParcelableArrayList, or SavedStateHandle["items"]); (2) Fragment arguments carrying a large model; (3) View hierarchy state from a large EditText or RecyclerView holding state; (4) multiple moderately large Bundles summing (activity + 3 fragments + view state); (5) a library storing a big blob in state. Red herring: device RAM, because the buffer is a fixed per-process 1 MB regardless of RAM.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with a heavy account; log Bundle sizes in a debug build by measuring Parcel.dataSize() of the saved Bundle per key (write a small helper). Use the TooLargeTool library (by Jake Wharton) in debug to log the top-level and per-key size at each onStop. Check adb logcat | grep -i "FAILED BINDER". Use Android Studio's "Do not keep activities" plus pressing Home to repro fast. Review the diff for onSaveInstanceState, SavedStateHandle, setArguments.
  5. Root cause: The carousel ViewModel saved its 600 items (each with title, description, image URL list) via SavedStateHandle, about 1.1 MB in Parcel form (Strings are UTF-16). On stop, the full saved Bundle goes to system_server in one Binder transaction, which exceeds the roughly 1 MB process buffer. Since API 24 the save happens at stop, so the user sees a crash after leaving, and it is data-dependent (long history = crash).
  6. Fix: Short-term: save only IDs (plus scroll position and filter selection) and reload from the repository/Room on restore; hotfix in 24 h. Long-term: treat saved state as UI-restoration pointers only; the data source of truth is Room/network; ViewModel keeps in-memory cache.
// Before
savedStateHandle["items"] = ArrayList(items)            // 1.1 MB
// After
savedStateHandle["itemIds"] = items.map { it.id }.take(50).toCollection(ArrayList())
  1. Prevention: Debug-build StrictMode-style check that logs a warning when saved state > 100 KB (TooLargeTool or custom ActivityLifecycleCallbacks measuring onActivityStopped/onSaveInstanceState); add the check to an instrumentation test that fills fake data, backgrounds the app and asserts no crash; Crashlytics alert on TransactionTooLargeException; code-review checklist item "no collections/Bitmaps/Serializable in state".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not catch the exception (it is thrown on a framework path outside my code). Not move to android:configChanges to avoid rotation, since this is unrelated. Not rely on a memory-cached ViewModel alone: after process death the cache is empty, so restoring IDs and reloading is still needed. The cost of the fix is an extra DB/network read on restore.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if the big thing is a Bitmap from the camera?" → Write it to a file in cache, keep the Uri/path in state; never put Bitmaps in Bundles.
  • "You reduced list state but the crash persists on a few devices" → Some other source: a View's own saved state (for example an unbounded TextView with freezesText, or RecyclerView custom saved state); measure per-view with a hierarchy dump of SparseArray.
  • "Can the crash happen with a 200 KB Bundle?" → Yes, if the buffer is already used by other in-flight transactions (for example big notification updates); the budget is process-wide.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A news app had this crash at 0.4% for months, dismissed as "OEM weirdness". It turned out an EditText for comment drafts froze 300 KB of text into view state plus a fragment argument holding a full article body; fixing both and adding a debug size logger dropped it to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests increasing buffer size or catching the exception; cannot explain why it happens at stop.
  • Hire: identifies saved state as the source, measures Bundle size, fixes by storing IDs and reloading.
  • Strong hire: explains process-wide shared buffer and UTF-16 overhead, API 24 stop timing, builds prevention (debug size logging, test, alert) and separates ViewModel cache from saved-state pointers.

questions.promptHtml: You need IPC between your app and a service in another process. When do you choose a local Binder, a Messenger, or AIDL?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A design-judgement question: do you pick the lightest mechanism and know its threading and concurrency limits?

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the service is in the same process, return a local Binder subclass: no IPC at all. For cross-process with simple request/response messages and no need for concurrency, use Messenger: it wraps a Handler, so all calls are serialised on one thread. For richer typed APIs, concurrent calls, return values, or multiple clients, use AIDL with a thread-safe implementation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Local Binder Messenger AIDL
Cross-process No Yes Yes
Typed methods / return values Yes (plain Kotlin) No, what/arg1/obj + Bundle Yes
Threading Caller's thread One Handler thread, serialised Binder pool, concurrent
Delivery semantic Direct call Effectively oneway (queued) Sync or oneway per method
Complexity Minimal Low Higher (codegen, versioning)
  • Messenger is built on an AIDL interface (IMessenger.send, declared oneway) wrapping a Handler. Replies go to msg.replyTo, another Messenger the client creates.
  • Message.obj can only carry Parcelable across processes (use setData(Bundle)); msg.sendingUid gives the caller's UID (verify trust before acting).
  • Serialisation is a feature when the service is not thread-safe, a limit under load (head-of-line blocking on the handler thread).
  • Ordering is guaranteed per Messenger; delivery is not confirmed.
  • Messenger cannot express errors the way exceptions do; you must design reply message types.
  • A local Binder only works in-process: android:process on the service breaks as MyBinder casts with ClassCastException (the remote returns a BinderProxy).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class EchoService : Service() {
    private val handler = object : Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) {
        override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
            val reply = Message.obtain(null, REPLY, msg.arg1 + 1, 0)
            try { msg.replyTo?.send(reply) } catch (e: RemoteException) { /* client died */ }
        }
    }
    private val messenger = Messenger(handler)
    override fun onBind(intent: Intent): IBinder = messenger.binder
    companion object { const val REPLY = 2 }
}
// Client: Messenger(binder).send(Message.obtain(null, 1, 41, 0).apply { replyTo = myMessenger })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Messenger for high-throughput streams (single-threaded, per-message overhead).
  • Putting non-Parcelable objects in msg.obj (works in-process, crashes cross-process).
  • Casting onServiceConnected's binder to a local class when the service is in another process.
  • Not validating sendingUid.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a Messenger service handle two clients concurrently? → No; the Handler serialises, though many clients can enqueue.
  2. How do you get results back? → Client's own Messenger passed in replyTo.
  3. How would you add auth? → Declare android:permission on the service plus check sendingUid/Binder.getCallingUid().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Messenger is easier than AIDL". Senior: threading model, oneway nature (no delivery guarantee), serialisation vs throughput, Parcelable-only payload, and the local-vs-remote binder cast trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A plug-in architecture used Messenger for a sensor stream; head-of-line blocking at 200 msgs/s lagged the UI until it was moved to AIDL with a coalescing callback.

questions.contextHtml:
A navigation app runs its routing engine in a bound service in android:process=":engine" (about 250 MB native memory). Clients bind from the UI process and call engine.reroute(req) (sync AIDL). Since v3.2, crash rate is 1.4% on low-RAM devices (3 GB), mostly after the user has been in other apps for a while:

android.os.DeadObjectException
    at android.os.BinderProxy.transactNative(Native Method)
    at com.acme.IEngine$Stub$Proxy.reroute(IEngine.java:112)
    at com.acme.nav.RouteRepo.reroute(RouteRepo.kt:58)

Logcat before it: ActivityManager: Killing 4123:com.acme.nav:engine (adj 900): empty #17 (lmkd kill) a few minutes earlier. QA never reproduces because their devices have 8 GB.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this crash happen, and how do you make the client robust?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception and retry once" with no reconnect logic, or "make the service foreground so it is never killed". Another weak response: restarting the app on error.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Is the client's ServiceConnection still holding the old proxy? (b) Did onServiceDisconnected fire? (c) Is the bind using BIND_AUTO_CREATE? (d) Is the call on the main thread or in a coroutine? (e) How does the engine restore state (route) after restart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap calls and on DeadObjectException rebind/wait for the new connection; ship as hotfix. Optionally lower the engine's memory footprint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Engine process killed by lmkd (log shows adj 900, cached/empty) while the client keeps a stale proxy; (2) engine crashed natively (check tombstones); (3) client never re-obtains binder after onServiceDisconnected; (4) race: call issued between death and reconnection. Red herring: the client's own memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell am kill com.acme.nav:engine in a test (or adb shell kill <pid>) reproduces deterministically; adb logcat -b all for lmkd/ActivityManager lines; adb shell dumpsys activity services com.acme.nav to see the connection state; check tombstones for native crash; unit test with a fake binder that throws DeadObjectException.
  5. Root cause: Cross-process binder is not a reliable reference: the remote process can die anytime. A sync call on a dead binder throws DeadObjectException (a RemoteException). The system calls onServiceDisconnected and, since the binding is BIND_AUTO_CREATE, restarts the service, giving a new binder via onServiceConnected. The code kept using the old proxy and treated RemoteException as impossible.
  6. Fix: Short-term: catch RemoteException at one boundary, mark disconnected, await the next onServiceConnected, retry idempotently. Long-term: an EngineClient that owns the connection state machine (Connected/Reconnecting), serialises requests, re-establishes session state (the engine must be restorable from the client's persisted route), registers a death recipient, and uses onBindingDied (API 28) to unbind and rebind.
private val conn = object : ServiceConnection {
    override fun onServiceConnected(n: ComponentName, b: IBinder) {
        engine = IEngine.Stub.asInterface(b); b.linkToDeath({ engine = null }, 0)
        resumeSession()
    }
    override fun onServiceDisconnected(n: ComponentName) { engine = null }  // will reconnect
    override fun onBindingDied(n: ComponentName) { unbind(); bind() }       // API 28+
}
suspend fun reroute(r: Req) = retryOnce { engine?.reroute(r) ?: throw IllegalStateException("not connected") }
  1. Prevention: Test with am kill in CI instrumentation; fault-injection fake service; Crashlytics custom key for engine connection state; lint/review rule: "any AIDL call must be in try/catch RemoteException through the client wrapper".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not make the engine a foreground service just to survive, since it costs a permanent notification and still can die (crash, OOM, user force-stop). Not retry non-idempotent calls blindly. Not block the main thread waiting for reconnect. Keeping a separate process costs memory and IPC but isolates native crashes; I would justify it with data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if the call is oneway?" → No exception for in-flight loss; add an acknowledgement or idempotent retry with sequence numbers.
  • "onServiceDisconnected never fired, but calls throw" → Possible if the binder died but the callback is posted on the main thread later; rely on exceptions plus linkToDeath.
  • "When does onBindingDied fire instead?" → When the hosting package is updated/removed or the user stops; the binding cannot be restored automatically.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A mapping app's out-of-process renderer died on memory pressure; the UI froze since the client retried the sync call in a loop on the main thread. Moving the client behind a state machine and coroutine retry with backoff made it invisible to users.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: catches and ignores, or wants foreground service as the fix.
  • Hire: explains stale proxy, reconnect via ServiceConnection, retry and test with am kill.
  • Strong hire: state machine, idempotency and session restore, death recipient vs onServiceDisconnected vs onBindingDied, and does not rely on keeping the process alive.

questions.contextHtml: A banking app's cold start p50 is 1.9 s, p95 3.4 s on mid-range devices (4 GB, Android 11-13). A trace (Perfetto) of Application.onCreate plus first Activity shows 410 ms on the main thread inside "binder transaction" slices. Breakdown: a feature-flag SDK calls packageManager.getPackageInfo(pkg, GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES) for each of 12 partner apps (about 14 ms each, 170 ms total), a device-fingerprint module calls getInstalledApplications(0) (about 60 ms, 400 apps), a root-check calls getInstalledPackages three times (about 150 ms), and ConnectivityManager.getActiveNetworkInfo() is called around 30 times by different layers (about 30 ms). Time on-CPU in the app is low. Product asks for p95 under 2.5 s.
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut this without removing the features?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move it all to a background thread" without checking whether startup needs the results, or "cache everything forever". Also optimising app code that is not the cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Which of these results are needed before first frame? (b) Can results be stale (package list changes rarely)? (c) Who owns each SDK, can I defer init? (d) What does each call return and how big is it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move non-critical calls off the startup path: feature flags and fingerprint run lazily after first frame on a background dispatcher.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Main thread blocked on synchronous Binder round trips (not CPU); (2) large result marshalling (getInstalledPackages sends hundreds of PackageInfo via ParceledListSlice, several transactions); (3) system_server contention under cold start (many apps starting); (4) repeated identical calls. Red herring: JIT/class loading (covered by A6 tooling).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto with binder_driver + sched categories: the main thread is in S (sleeping) state under "binder transaction"; the server-side slice shows PackageManagerService work. Use dumpsys binder_calls_stats (debuggable) or add timing around SDK calls. Count call sites with a stack-sampling run or an Android Studio profiler system trace.
  5. Root cause: Each Manager method is a synchronous Binder call to system_server; the main thread sleeps until the reply. Per-call cost is small (hundreds of microseconds when idle) but goes to milliseconds when system_server is busy with cold-start traffic, and bulk calls multiply payload and marshalling cost. Thirty identical getActiveNetworkInfo() calls are pure waste.
  6. Fix: Short-term: (a) memoise per-process caches for network state using a registered NetworkCallback (push, zero IPC on read); (b) replace the 12 getPackageInfo calls with one cached package query, or defer them off the startup path; (c) dedupe the three package listings to one cached result persisted for the version/lastUpdateTime; (d) run the rest on Dispatchers.Default after first frame. Long-term: a startup budget: "no Binder calls on the main thread before first frame unless approved", with App Startup initializers lazy where possible.
class NetState(cm: ConnectivityManager) {
    @Volatile var online = false
    init { cm.registerDefaultNetworkCallback(object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
        override fun onAvailable(n: Network) { online = true }
        override fun onLost(n: Network) { online = false }
    }) }
}
  1. Prevention: Macrobenchmark startup test with a regression threshold; trace-based CI check counting Binder slices on main thread; code review rule that wraps Manager calls in the app's own cached facade. (Profiling playbooks themselves belong to the startup track.)
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not cache package lists indefinitely (installs/uninstalls change them; invalidate on ACTION_PACKAGE_* broadcast or lastUpdateTime). Not block with runBlocking to "make it async". Package visibility (API 30+) also filters results, so behaviour may differ per device; I would verify with <queries>.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Every call is 0.4 ms, so why 410 ms?" → Counting: about 100 calls plus bulk list marshalling, plus contention; per-call average hides the tail.
  • "Could you make the calls from a background thread but still need results at launch?" → Then overlap them with other init work and join before first use; the saving is parallelism, not elimination.
  • "What about oneway?" → Not an option; these APIs return values.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shopping app lost 250 ms at startup to a "who is installed" check that three SDKs each ran; consolidating into one cached call and deferring two SDKs recovered most of it without touching features.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "use a background thread" without diagnosis.
  • Hire: identifies Binder round-trips from trace, dedupes and defers calls, caches.
  • Strong hire: explains per-call vs bulk costs, ParceledListSlice, server contention, push-based NetworkCallback, package visibility effects, and sets a guardrail (benchmarks, review rule).

questions.promptHtml: How do you detect and handle the death of a process you hold a Binder reference to? Cover linkToDeath, DeadObjectException, and RemoteCallbackList.
