sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Resource leaks and ghost callbacks in multi-process designs come from not handling peer death. This separates people who have built a real IPC service.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The driver tracks references. On a remote IBinder I can call linkToDeath(recipient, 0) and get binderDied() on a Binder thread when the hosting process dies; synchronous calls to a dead binder throw DeadObjectException. On the server side, a client callback is just a proxy, so I store callbacks in a RemoteCallbackList, which links to death for each entry, removes dead ones automatically and gives me a safe broadcast loop.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• When a process exits, the kernel closes its binder fd and the driver sends death notifications (BR_DEAD_BINDER) to every process that registered interest (BC_REQUEST_DEATH_NOTIFICATION) on that node. libbinder delivers it to Java DeathRecipient.binderDied().
  • linkToDeath throws RemoteException if the binder is already dead; that is the race handling you must code. It only makes sense on a proxy (remote binder); on a local Binder it does nothing useful.
  • Callback runs on a Binder thread, not main. Post to your own executor/Looper before touching state. API 30 added binderDied(IBinder who) as an overload to tell which binder died.
  • isBinderAlive() and pingBinder() are point-in-time hints and racy; use them for diagnostics, not correctness.
  • Exceptions: sync call to dead process: DeadObjectException. System server death: DeadSystemException (subclass). Oneway call to a dead process already known to the driver may fail immediately; if the process dies after delivery, the message is lost silently.
  • RemoteCallbackList<E: IInterface>: register(cb) returns false if already dead; unregister; beginBroadcast() / getBroadcastItem(i) / finishBroadcast() must be paired; overriding onCallbackDied(cb) lets you clean per-client state; kill() on service destroy. Compared with an ArrayList<IFooCallback>: the list leaks dead proxies and throws on each broadcast.
  • Death of the client matters to the server: release locks, stop streaming, free native resources. Death of the server matters to clients: reconnect (see the DeadObjectException scenario).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val callbacks = RemoteCallbackList<IRecorderCallback>()

override fun register(cb: IRecorderCallback) { callbacks.register(cb) }
override fun unregister(cb: IRecorderCallback) { callbacks.unregister(cb) }

private fun dispatch(state: Int) {
    val n = callbacks.beginBroadcast()
    try {
        for (i in 0 until n) {
            try { callbacks.getBroadcastItem(i).onState(state) }
            catch (e: RemoteException) { /* RemoteCallbackList removes dead entries itself */ }
        }
    } finally { callbacks.finishBroadcast() }
}

// Client side watching the server
val death = IBinder.DeathRecipient { handler.post { onServerDied() } }
try { binder.linkToDeath(death, 0) } catch (e: RemoteException) { onServerDied() } // already dead

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutating UI or shared state directly in binderDied.
  • Forgetting finishBroadcast() (leaks internal state).
  • Holding a plain MutableList<Callback>.
  • Calling a client callback synchronously inside a lock (a hung client freezes the server; prefer oneway callbacks).
  • Never calling unlinkToDeath (leaks the recipient and strong references).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why should callbacks be oneway? → A slow or hung client otherwise blocks the broadcasting thread; oneway queues without waiting.
  2. Does death notification fire if the app is merely "stopped/killed" by the user? → Yes; any process death closes the binder fd. The freezer (cached apps frozen on Android 11+) is not death; frozen processes still exist, oneway calls to them are queued.
  3. How do you avoid the register/death race? → Handle the exception from linkToDeath immediately as "already dead".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE has seen DeadObjectException. Senior designs both directions: death recipients on the client, RemoteCallbackList on the server, correct threading of binderDied, and idempotent reconnect.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A music service kept an ArrayList of UI callbacks; clients that crashed stayed forever, every progress tick threw DeadObjectException, and CPU burned at 100% on one binder thread.

questions.contextHtml: A document-scanning app moves its ML pipeline into an isolated process (android:process=":ml", isolatedProcess="true") for crash and security isolation. The UI process sends camera frames (1920x1080 YUV, about 3.1 MB each; 12 fps preview) to :ml and receives detections (about 2 KB). The first prototype passes ByteArray through AIDL. On a mid-range device you see TransactionTooLargeException immediately, and when downscaled to 640x480 (about 460 KB) frames are accepted but preview jank is 18% of frames, and 2-3% of sessions throw DeadObjectException when the ML process is killed. Product wants full-resolution captures (up to 12 MP JPEG, 4-6 MB) to be processed too.
questions.promptHtml: Design the data path between the two processes. What do you send through Binder, what not, and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Split the array into 500 KB chunks and send many transactions" (shares the same process-wide buffer and copies everything twice) or "use a file for everything" without thinking about latency and cleanup.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Is the ML process required to see every frame or can it drop frames (latest wins)? (b) Is it the same app (same signature), so I can share FDs freely? (c) Is latency or throughput more important? (d) Does the output need to be ordered or acknowledged? (e) What is the min API level (SharedMemory needs API 27)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce frame size and rate for now (analysis at 640x480, 5 fps) and drop frames when the ML process is busy, so the UI never blocks.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The design problem: a Binder transaction copies bytes into the destination's 1 MB process buffer, so a 3.1 MB frame cannot fit and 460 KB frames at 12 fps churn the buffer, with sync calls blocking the camera thread. The right model is to share memory, and use Binder only for signalling and small metadata.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto trace for binder transactions per frame and time per transaction; dumpsys meminfo for both processes to verify shared memory shows as shared; a debug counter of dropped frames; kill :ml via adb shell am kill for DeadObject handling; measure with 12 MP images for peak memory.
  5. Root cause: Using Binder as a bulk data pipe. Binder is optimised for small RPCs; payload size is capped by the shared buffer and each transaction is a copy.
  6. Fix (the design):
    • Frames (streaming): Allocate a ring buffer of N=3 slots in SharedMemory (API 27+; backed by ashmem/memfd). Pass the SharedMemory object (a Parcelable that carries an FD) to :ml once at session start. For each frame, the producer writes into a free slot with mapReadWrite() and sends only a oneway message onFrame(slotIndex, seq, w, h, ts). :ml maps read-only, processes, and sends onSlotFree(slotIndex) back. If no free slot, drop the frame. Zero bulk copies through Binder.
    • High-res stills: Write the JPEG to app cache and pass a ParcelFileDescriptor (opened read-only) through AIDL; :ml reads from the FD. No URI permissions needed because FDs are capabilities; with other apps use a ContentProvider/FileProvider with grantUriPermissions.
    • Streams of unknown length: ParcelFileDescriptor.createPipe() and write on a background thread; remember to close both ends.
    • Bitmap: Bitmap is Parcelable and bigger ones are marshalled via ashmem blobs, but the transaction still holds an FD and a copy semantic; I would not rely on it for streaming.
    • Results: a small Parcelable (2 KB) in a oneway callback.
val shm = SharedMemory.create("frames", SLOTS * FRAME_BYTES)
val writer: ByteBuffer = shm.mapReadWrite()             // producer
ml.attach(shm)                                          // AIDL: Parcelable FD passed once
// per frame (no bulk Binder):
writer.position(slot * FRAME_BYTES); writer.put(yuv)
ml.onFrame(slot, seq, w, h, ts)                         // oneway, ~40 bytes

Synchronisation: shared memory has no built-in locks. I use the slot ownership protocol (producer owns until onFrame, consumer until onSlotFree) and sequence numbers to detect stale reads. 7. Prevention: Fault-injection tests (kill :ml mid-frame; recreate shared memory and re-attach on reconnect); a benchmark with frame-rate and drop-rate assertions; static check forbidding ByteArray over a size threshold in AIDL (review rule: "AIDL params must be small"). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not chunking big arrays through Binder: it uses the shared buffer, adds latency and complexity. Shared memory adds a custom protocol and memory-safety risks (the reader sees whatever the writer writes; treat as untrusted if cross-trust). Files add disk I/O but are simplest for stills. Fallback for API < 27: MemoryFile via reflection is hidden-API risk; I would use pipes/files instead. Zero-copy GPU paths (HardwareBuffer, API 26) are an option if frames are GPU-resident.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "The ML process dies mid-stream" → Reconnect, recreate or re-send the SharedMemory FD, reset slot ownership, bump a generation id so late onSlotFree is ignored.
  • "Why oneway for onFrame?" → The camera thread must not block on ML; ordering per binder object is preserved.
  • "Is SharedMemory visible to other apps?" → Only if you pass the FD; FDs through Binder are capabilities, which is why they are safer than world-readable files.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A video filter app sent each frame through a bound service as a byte[] and hit jank plus rare TransactionTooLarge on foldables with higher-res cameras; switching to a shared-memory ring and oneway signalling cut p95 frame time dramatically and removed the crash class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chunking through Binder; or cannot explain the 1 MB limit.
  • Hire: proposes file/FD or shared memory with Binder for metadata only.
  • Strong hire: ring buffer with ownership protocol, oneway signalling, drop policy, death/reconnect handling, API level constraints and security considerations.

questions.promptHtml: In a service that other apps can bind to, how do you know who is calling and enforce permissions? Explain getCallingUid, enforceCallingPermission, checkCallingOrSelfPermission and clearCallingIdentity.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Exported IPC endpoints are an attack surface. Getting caller identity wrong is a classic confused-deputy vulnerability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The kernel stamps each Binder transaction with the sender's UID and PID, and Binder.getCallingUid() returns it on the Binder thread handling that call. For access control I use <service android:permission="..."> (enforced when binding) plus per-method checks with enforceCallingPermission against a signature-level permission. I avoid checkCallingOrSelfPermission for security checks, because my own process usually holds the permission, so it passes. clearCallingIdentity resets the identity to my own so downstream calls run as me; it must be restored in a finally block.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Identity is thread-local to the transaction. On a Binder thread during a call, getCallingUid() is the sender. On any other thread (for example one you post work to), it returns your own UID, so checks done there are meaningless. Capture the UID on entry.
  • PID is racy: processes die and PIDs are reused. Authorise by UID (and package/signature), not PID.
  • Methods:
    API Meaning
    Context.checkCallingPermission(p) Caller must hold p; returns DENIED if not in a Binder transaction
    Context.checkCallingOrSelfPermission(p) Caller or this process holds p; own process holds its own declared permission, so almost always granted
    enforceCallingPermission(p, msg) Throws SecurityException if the caller lacks p
    Binder.clearCallingIdentity() / restoreCallingIdentity(token) Make downstream calls as self; system services use it heavily
  • Layers of control: android:exported, android:permission on the component (checked by system_server on bind/start), a custom permission with android:protectionLevel="signature" (only apps signed with your key can get it), then in-method checks for finer-grained rules (per-user, per-package).
  • Package spoofing: a caller can claim any String pkg argument. Verify with packageManager.getPackagesForUid(Binder.getCallingUid()) containing pkg (and signature via PackageManager signing info if needed).
  • Messenger: msg.sendingUid.
  • Confused deputy: your service has privileges (permissions, file access); if a caller can make it act on arbitrary targets (a path, a URI, an Intent), it uses your privileges on their behalf. Validate and, when forwarding to another component, clearCallingIdentity is the wrong tool; use the caller's identity (or check checkUriPermission with the caller UID).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Manifest
// <permission android:name="com.acme.permission.ADMIN" android:protectionLevel="signature"/>
// <service android:name=".AdminService" android:exported="true" android:permission="com.acme.permission.ADMIN"/>

private val binder = object : IAdmin.Stub() {
    override fun wipe(pkg: String) {
        val uid = Binder.getCallingUid()
        enforceCallingPermission("com.acme.permission.ADMIN", "wipe")
        require(packageManager.getPackagesForUid(uid)?.contains(pkg) == true) { "pkg spoof" }
        val token = Binder.clearCallingIdentity()
        try { doPrivilegedWipe(pkg) } finally { Binder.restoreCallingIdentity(token) }
    }
}

Broken: if (checkCallingOrSelfPermission(P) == GRANTED) doWipe(): always true.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using checkCallingOrSelfPermission or checkSelfPermission for authorisation.
  • Checking the identity on a worker thread after handing off.
  • Trusting the package name in the arguments.
  • Leaving clearCallingIdentity without restore (identity leaks into the thread's later transactions).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is android:permission on the service enough? → It gates binding, not each call; after binding, any method is callable. Add per-method checks if tiers exist.
  2. How do you restrict to your own apps only? → Signature-level custom permission, or compare calling UID's signing certificate hash.
  3. What about isolated processes? → They have a distinct isolated UID; do not authorise based on UID equality with your app; use the owning app via the binder you handed out.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "add exported=false or a permission". Senior reasons about identity per thread, UID vs PID, OrSelf pitfalls, argument spoofing, signature permissions and confused deputy.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech SDK ships in the host app com.acme.wallet (3M installs). Partner apps bind to its service to request a payment. A bug bounty report says any app on the device can read the user's last 10 transactions and trigger a refund. Here is the shipped code:

// AndroidManifest.xml
// <permission android:name="com.acme.PAY" android:protectionLevel="normal"/>
// <service android:name=".PayService" android:exported="true"/>

class PayService : Service() {
    private val executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()

    private val binder = object : IPay.Stub() {
        override fun lastTransactions(callerPkg: String): List<Txn> {
            if (checkCallingOrSelfPermission("com.acme.PAY") != PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED)
                throw SecurityException("no")
            return repo.last(10, callerPkg)
        }
        override fun refund(txnId: String, cb: IPayCallback) {
            executor.execute {
                if (checkCallingPermission("com.acme.PAY") == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) {
                    cb.onDone(repo.refund(txnId))
                }
            }
        }
    }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent): IBinder = binder
}

Logcat in the bounty PoC shows the attacker app calling both methods successfully from uid=10247 (not signed with your key). Red herring: the team had just enabled R8 and thought "obfuscation broke permission checks".
questions.promptHtml: List every flaw, explain why the attack works, and fix it. How do you prevent this class in future?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spots only "missing permission on the service". Misses the thread issue, the OrSelf pitfall and the package-name spoof. Fixes with exported=false, breaking partner integrations.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Do partners come from known signing keys? (b) How many partner versions are in the field? (c) Is a refund idempotent and does it have server-side auth? (d) Do we have logs of exploitation (server-side audit trail)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side: require re-auth/step-up for refunds and rate-limit; patch the app with at least android:permission and signature-level protection; if exploitation is suspected, disable the service remotely (feature flag in onBind returning null) and notify per policy. Coordinate disclosure and bounty.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (the flaws):
    1. Permission declared normal: any app can request it in its manifest and is granted at install; no signature restriction.
    2. No android:permission attribute on the <service>; any app can bind (exported=true).
    3. checkCallingOrSelfPermission: our process holds com.acme.PAY (we declared it), so the "or self" half is always granted: the check is vacuous even in the happy case.
    4. In refund, the check runs on a worker thread: Binder.getCallingUid() there is our own UID, so checkCallingPermission evaluates our own process or returns denied depending on identity; the logic is unreliable and wrong. (Combined with the previous point the check is meaningless.) The intended check must happen on the Binder thread at entry.
    5. callerPkg is client-supplied: the attacker passes the victim partner's package and reads that partner's transactions: a spoof (IDOR).
    6. cb.onDone is called from the worker without handling RemoteException and the callback runs in our process holding no limit; plus the callback is unauthenticated (attacker-controlled binder).
  4. How I'd verify each: Write a PoC attacker APK (different signature) that requests the normal permission and binds; run adb shell dumpsys package com.acme.wallet to read the permission's protection level; aapt dump xmltree/apkanalyzer manifest print to see exported components; add a unit test that mocks Binder.getCallingUid(); check with MobSF or Android Lint "ExportedService" and "ProtectedPermissions".
  5. Root cause: Authorisation relied on an app-defined normal permission (anyone can hold it) and on a check that always passes or runs on the wrong thread, with the caller's identity taken from an argument.
  6. Fix:
// <permission android:name="com.acme.PAY" android:protectionLevel="signature"/>
// <service android:name=".PayService" android:exported="true" android:permission="com.acme.PAY"/>
override fun lastTransactions(): List<Txn> {
    enforceCallingPermission("com.acme.PAY", "lastTransactions")  // on the Binder thread
    val uid = Binder.getCallingUid()
    val pkg = packageManager.getPackagesForUid(uid)!!.first()
    return repo.last(10, pkg)                                    // derive identity, do not accept it
}
override fun refund(txnId: String, cb: IPayCallback) {
    enforceCallingPermission("com.acme.PAY", "refund")           // before hand-off
    val uid = Binder.getCallingUid()
    executor.execute {
        val res = repo.refund(txnId, requesterUid = uid)         // authorise by captured uid + server-side
        try { cb.onDone(res) } catch (_: RemoteException) {}
    }
}

For third-party partners (different signatures) use a signature-or-allowlist model: verify the calling package's signing certificate hash against server-provided allowlist, or require an OAuth-style token issued per partner. 7. Prevention: Threat-model each exported component in design review; Lint checks (ExportedService, ProtectedPermissions); automated test that installs a differently-signed test APK and asserts denial; security regression test in CI; periodic dumpsys package audit of merged manifest; bug bounty follow-up. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not set exported=false (it breaks legitimate partners; use signature permission or allowlist). Not use PID for identity. Not rely on obfuscation or "hidden" action strings. Signature permissions limit partners to apps signed with our key; broader partner support needs allowlisting with certificate pinning, adding operational cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "A partner is signed by their own key" → Allowlist (package + certificate SHA-256) fetched from our backend, verified in the service; or a per-partner token the partner obtains from our server, verified on each call.
  • "After the fix, old partner builds crash" → They lacked the permission; stage rollout with a compatibility window, still-gated refunds first (higher risk), reads second.
  • "Can the attacker still DoS us?" → Yes, via binds; add rate limiting and quotas per UID.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An internal audit of a payments SDK found a service whose checks passed for every caller; no exploitation occurred, but the fix required a staged permission migration over three partner release cycles.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only notices "exported without permission".
  • Hire: finds normal-level permission, OrSelf pitfall and the spoofed package parameter, proposes signature permission.
  • Strong hire: also catches the worker-thread identity bug, designs derived-identity and allowlist for third parties, adds test strategy, rollout plan and DoS considerations.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what happens, from the Kotlin call to the kernel and back, when app A makes a synchronous Binder call to a service in app B. What is mapped, what is copied, and which threads are involved?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A staff-level "do you really understand it" question. It exposes whether the candidate can reason about blocking, copy cost, buffer limits and death notification from first principles.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Kotlin call goes to a Proxy that writes arguments into a Parcel and calls BinderProxy.transact, which goes through JNI to libbinder IPCThreadState, then an ioctl(BINDER_WRITE_READ) on /dev/binder. The driver finds the target by handle, copies the Parcel data once into the buffer that B mapped at startup, wakes a Binder thread in B (spawning one if needed), and B runs Stub.onTransact. The reply goes back the same way; A's thread sleeps in the driver the whole time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App A (client thread T)                Kernel binder driver              App B
Proxy.method(args)
 -> Parcel.write*                                                       (mmap'd read-only
 -> BinderProxy.transact (JNI)                                           ~1 MB buffer, set
 -> BpBinder::transact                                                   up at process start)
 -> IPCThreadState::transact
 -> ioctl(BINDER_WRITE_READ) -------> BC_TRANSACTION
                                      look up handle -> binder_node of B
                                      allocate buffer in B's mmap area
                                      copy_from_user(A data) -> that buffer   (the ONE copy)
                                      translate objects: handles, FDs (dup'd)
                                      stamp sender uid/pid
                                      pick idle thread in B; BR_SPAWN_LOOPER if none
                                      T sleeps, waiting reply
                                                      ------> BR_TRANSACTION on B's Binder thread
                                                              JavaBBinder -> Binder.execTransact
                                                              -> Stub.onTransact -> your code
                                      <------ BC_REPLY (copy back into A's buffer)
 <- BR_REPLY; T wakes; Parcel.read*
                                      BC_FREE_BUFFER (B frees; A frees reply buffer)

Key points:

  • mmap: at startup each process maps about 1 MB of kernel-allocated pages (ProcessState), read-only to userspace. The driver writes incoming data directly into the receiver's mapped pages, so the receiver reads without a second copy. That is the "one copy" claim.
  • Handles and references: objects are identified in the driver by binder_node (owner side) and binder_ref (per-process handle). Handle 0 is the service manager. Passing an IBinder in a Parcel makes the driver create a new ref in the receiver and translate the handle. Reference counts keep the node alive; releasing the last ref lets the owner garbage-collect.
  • FDs: passed as file descriptor objects; the driver duplicates them into the receiver's table (that is how ParcelFileDescriptor and SharedMemory cross).
  • Buffer lifetime: the receiver's buffer for a transaction is held until it frees it (BC_FREE_BUFFER); long-lived in-flight work pins the space.
  • Threads: client thread blocks; server runs on pool thread; the driver may set the server thread's priority/nice to the caller's for sync calls (priority inheritance).
  • Death notification: when a process's fd closes, the driver releases its nodes and sends BR_DEAD_BINDER to processes that registered death interest; pending sync calls to it complete with a dead-reply error (DeadObjectException).
  • Security: SELinux hooks check binder_call, so a transaction can be refused regardless of Android permissions; UID/PID/security context come from the kernel.
  • Debugging windows: Perfetto binder events and binder_driver atrace category; /sys/kernel/debug/binder and binderfs state on rooted/debug builds; dumpsys from adb shell for services. Platform has also separate nodes: /dev/hwbinder (HIDL/AIDL HAL), /dev/vndbinder (vendor); Android 10+ uses binderfs to mount multiple Binder devices.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Observing it (not production code)

# Perfetto / atrace categories to see binder activity
adb shell atrace --async_start -b 16384 binder_driver sched
adb shell atrace --async_stop -z > trace.gz   # open in ui.perfetto.dev: look for "binder transaction"/"binder reply" slices
adb logcat | grep -i "FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying Binder is "zero copy" or "uses shared memory". It is one copy into receiver pages that the receiver mapped.
  • Forgetting that the client thread blocks (and with it, the main thread if you called from there).
  • Treating oneway as free: it still copies and uses the async half of the buffer.
  • Thinking Binder permission checks are only Android permissions: SELinux also applies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does a Binder call from the UI thread to a busy service cause jank? → The UI thread sleeps until a server thread executes and replies; priority inheritance helps CPU but not lock waits on the server.
  2. What bounds concurrency? → Binder thread pool of the server (default max about 15 spawned) and buffer space.
  3. How do death notifications work if the process is killed by lmkd? → Same path: process exit closes the fd, the driver notifies.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE describes Proxy/Stub. Senior can narrate the data path through libbinder and the driver, name where the copy happens, explain handles/refcounts/death and tie each to a real-world symptom (jank, TransactionTooLarge, DeadObject).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Reading a Perfetto trace where the UI thread is sleeping inside a "binder transaction" and the server-side thread is waiting on a lock is how many "mysterious" main-thread stalls get root-caused.

questions.contextHtml:
You own com.acme.pay, a host app exposing an AIDL service used by 40 partner apps (about 2M combined installs; partners update on their own schedule, host updates roll weekly). Current AIDL:

interface IPay {
    PayResult pay(in PayRequest req);       // code 1
    void cancel(String id);                 // code 2
    int status(String id);                  // code 3
}
// PayRequest.java (hand-written Parcelable): writes amount, currency, merchant

The team wants to add refund(String id, long amountMinor) and a new field idempotencyKey to PayRequest. A junior dev inserted refund between pay and cancel "for readability" and added idempotencyKey in the middle of writeToParcel. In the staging mix test, an old partner build (built against the old AIDL) calling cancel() against the new host caused a refund; another old client crashed with RuntimeException: Parcel android.os.Parcel@...: Unmarshalling unknown type code when reading a PayRequest. Rollout to prod starts Monday.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, how do you migrate safely with clients on both old and new versions, and how do you stop this recurring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just force partners to update" (impossible on your schedule) or "tell partners to rebuild"; no understanding of transaction codes; adding fields to a Parcelable without version handling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Which skew directions exist: old client/new host (certain) and new client/old host (possible if host updates lag)? (b) Is the AIDL distributed as source to partners or as a library? (c) Can I tell the client version from the server (calling package version)? (d) Are payments idempotent server-side?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the Monday rollout. Revert the AIDL to the shipped layout. Money-moving mismatch (cancel executing refund) is a P0.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Transaction codes are positional: code = FIRST_CALL_TRANSACTION + method index, so inserting refund as method 2 shifted cancel to 3 and status to 4: an old client sending code 2 now hits refund. (2) The hand-written Parcelable has no version/length prefix; readers consume fields in order, so an inserted field shifts everything after it. (3) An extra red herring: R8; irrelevant since AIDL codes are baked in at generation. (4) Missing dispatch for unknown transactions.
  4. How I'd verify each: Decompile both generated stubs (IPay$Stub) to compare constants TRANSACTION_cancel; instrument the staging host to log the incoming code; write a unit test reading a golden byte array of the old PayRequest; run old-client/new-host and new-client/old-host matrix on a device pair.
  5. Root cause: Wire compatibility was treated as source compatibility. AIDL/Binder has no method names on the wire (just integer codes) and the hand-written Parcelable has no framing, so any non-append change is a breaking change.
  6. Fix:
    • AIDL: append only. Never reorder or remove; deprecate in place.
interface IPay {
    int apiVersion();           // see below: first-ever added at the END for now (can't be first retroactively)
    PayResult pay(in PayRequest req);   // 1
    void cancel(String id);             // 2
    int status(String id);              // 3
    void refund(String id, long amountMinor); // 4 (appended)
    int apiVersion();                   // 5 (appended), clients call it before using refund
}
  • Parcelable: new version writes a leading length/version and appends new fields at the end, reading with bounds checks; or switch to carrying a Bundle of named values (forward-compatible by design).
override fun writeToParcel(p: Parcel, f: Int) {
    val start = p.dataPosition(); p.writeInt(0)         // length placeholder
    p.writeLong(amount); p.writeString(currency); p.writeString(merchant)
    p.writeString(idempotencyKey)                       // appended in v2
    val end = p.dataPosition(); p.setDataPosition(start); p.writeInt(end - start); p.setDataPosition(end)
}
private constructor(p: Parcel) { val start = p.dataPosition(); val len = p.readInt()
    amount = p.readLong(); currency = p.readString()!!; merchant = p.readString()!!
    idempotencyKey = if (p.dataPosition() - start < len) p.readString() else null
    p.setDataPosition(start + len) }
  • Client-side degradation: new clients call apiVersion() once, wrapped in try/catch, and only use refund if >= 2. For new methods called on an old host, transact returns false for an unknown code and generated proxies fall back to a default implementation if one was set with Stub.setDefaultImpl (verify the generated code in your build-tools version); otherwise guard by version check.
  • Rollout: ship host with the append-only AIDL, hold refund behind a flag, then enable after the partner cohort is compatible. Dual-support period with explicit minimum-client policy.
  1. Prevention: Check the .aidl into a contract/ directory and a CI job that diffs the AIDL against the released baseline and fails on non-append changes; golden-file Parcel tests for every released version; compatibility matrix instrumentation test (N-1, N-2 clients vs head host); release notes and deprecation policy for partners; Perfetto/logs in the host that report the caller's package version and which API versions are in use.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "readability" ordering ever; AIDL is a binary protocol. Not rely on parcelables to be evolvable without framing. Bundles are flexible but lose type safety; I would use them for the extensible request payload and keep methods few and coarse. Not ship the new method without the version handshake. Cost: a permanent legacy surface until the minimum supported partner version moves.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "A partner recompiled with the new AIDL but the user has the old host" → Version check (apiVersion()), or default impl; the app must degrade gracefully.
  • "Can you rename a method?" → Yes at the source level, wire code unchanged; the name is not on the wire, but doing so across the partner SDKs breaks their compile, so keep the old name.
  • "How do you retire cancel?" → Keep the code slot forever; make it throw UnsupportedOperationException (a marshalled exception) after the sunset date.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments SDK team discovered during a staged rollout that readability-driven reordering swapped cancel and refund; thanks to staged rollout and server-side idempotency no money moved wrongly, and a CI AIDL diff gate became mandatory afterward.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: does not understand positional transaction codes; proposes forced updates.
  • Hire: append-only AIDL, version/length handling for Parcelable, rollback and staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: compatibility matrix, version handshake plus default impl, bundles for extensibility, CI gate on AIDL diff, deprecation policy and server-side idempotency as a safety net.
